title: Activation functions (ReLU, GELU, why not linear)
summary: Without a bend between them, stacked linear layers collapse into a single linear layer. The sigmoid bends but its flat tails starve learning; ReLU keeps a slope of 1 wherever it is active; GELU is a smooth ReLU used in GPT-2 and BERT. Sums of shifted hinges can trace almost any curve.
llm_link: GPT-2 and BERT use GELU in their feed-forward layers, and many recent models use a gated variant called SwiGLU. Without these bends, a hundred transformer blocks would be no more expressive than one matrix.
key_ideas: W2(W1x + b1) + b2 = (W2W1)x + (W2b1 + b2): two linear layers are one linear layer, however many you stack.
Sigmoid squeezes into (0, 1); its slope is at most 1/4 and almost 0 in the tails, so learning signals fade.
ReLU = max(0, z): slope 1 when active, 0 when not. A neuron that is negative for every input is dead and stops learning.
Shifted, scaled ReLUs add up to tents, bumps and any curve made of straight pieces.
GELU(z) = z·Φ(z): like ReLU for large |z|, smooth near 0, with a small dip to about −0.17.

quiz.q: You stack 50 layers with no activation functions. What can the network represent?
options: Only what a single linear layer (Wx + b) can
quiz.explain: Multiplying out the algebra merges all the matrices into one matrix and all the biases into one bias.

quiz.q: Predict the result: what is the largest slope the sigmoid ever has?
quiz.explain: σ'(z) = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)), which peaks at z = 0 where σ = 1/2, giving 1/2 · 1/2 = 1/4.

quiz.q: Predict the result: f(x) = ReLU(x + 1) − 2·ReLU(x) + ReLU(x − 1). What is f(0.5)?
quiz.explain: ReLU(1.5) − 2·ReLU(0.5) + ReLU(−0.5) = 1.5 − 1 + 0 = 0.5. This is the tent from the video, peaking at 1 when x = 0.

options: If its input is negative for every example, its slope is 0 everywhere and it gets no learning signal
quiz.explain: On the flat side the slope is zero, so backpropagation sends nothing to its weights and nothing can move it back.

quiz.q: Which activation does GPT-2 use in its feed-forward layers?
quiz.explain: GPT-2 (and BERT) use GELU, a smooth version of ReLU. Many newer models use the gated SwiGLU.

problems.title: Three bends and their slopes
problems.prompt:
Write each activation and its slope (derivative). Use math only.

  • sigmoid(z) and sigmoid_slope(z) = sigmoid(z) * (1 - sigmoid(z))
  • relu(z) and relu_slope(z): 1 if z > 0 else 0
  • gelu(z) = z · Φ(z) with Φ(z) = 0.5 · (1 + erf(z / √2)); math.erf exists.

tests.name: sigmoid
tests.code: assert sigmoid(0) == 0.5, f'sigmoid(0) should be 0.5, got {sigmoid(0)}'

tests.name: sigmoid slope peaks at 1/4
tests.code:
s = sigmoid_slope(0)
assert s is not None and abs(s - 0.25) < 1e-9, f'the steepest point is z = 0 with slope 0.25, got {s}'
assert sigmoid_slope(6) < 0.003, f'far out in the tail the slope should be almost 0, got {sigmoid_slope(6)}'

tests.name: relu and its slope
tests.code:
assert relu(-3) == 0 and relu(2.5) == 2.5, 'relu keeps positives and zeroes negatives'
assert relu_slope(4) == 1 and relu_slope(-4) == 0, f'slope should be 1 when active and 0 when not, got {relu_slope(4)} and {relu_slope(-4)}'

tests.name: gelu is like relu far from zero
tests.code:
g = gelu(5)
assert g is not None and abs(g - 5) < 1e-4, f'gelu(5) should be almost 5, got {g}'
assert abs(gelu(-5)) < 1e-4, f'gelu(-5) should be almost 0, got {gelu(-5)}'

tests.name: gelu dips below zero
tests.code:
m = min(gelu(x / 100) for x in range(-300, 1))
assert -0.18 < m < -0.16, f'GELU dips to about -0.17 near z = -0.75, your minimum is {m}'

problems.title: Two linear layers are one (NumPy)
problems.prompt:
Write collapse(W1, b1, W2, b2) that returns the single (W, b) with W @ x + b == W2 @ (W1 @ x + b1) + b2 for every x. Multiply out the algebra from the video.

Then check(x, W1, b1, W2, b2) should return True when the two-layer and one-layer outputs agree (use np.allclose).
problems.starter:
import numpy as np

def collapse(W1, b1, W2, b2):
    # TODO: W = ?, b = ?
    W = None
    b = None
    return W, b

def check(x, W1, b1, W2, b2):
    W, b = collapse(W1, b1, W2, b2)
    two = W2 @ (W1 @ x + b1) + b2
    one = W @ x + b
    return np.allclose(two, one)

tests.name: collapses random layers
tests.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
W1, b1 = rng.normal(size=(4, 3)), rng.normal(size=4)
W2, b2 = rng.normal(size=(2, 4)), rng.normal(size=2)
W, b = collapse(W1, b1, W2, b2)
assert W is not None and b is not None, 'collapse returned None'
assert W.shape == (2, 3), f'3 inputs, 2 outputs: W should be (2, 3), got {W.shape}. Order matters: W2 @ W1, not W1 @ W2'
for _ in range(5):
    x = rng.normal(size=3)
    assert check(x, W1, b1, W2, b2), 'one-layer and two-layer outputs differ; the bias is W2 @ b1 + b2'

tests.name: bias goes through the second matrix
tests.code:
import numpy as np
W1, b1 = np.eye(2), np.array([1.0, 0.0])
W2, b2 = np.array([[2.0, 0.0], [0.0, 3.0]]), np.zeros(2)
W, b = collapse(W1, b1, W2, b2)
assert np.allclose(b, [2, 0]), f'b1 = [1, 0] passes through W2, giving [2, 0]; got {b}'

problems.title: Build a bump from hinges
problems.prompt:
Build curves out of ReLUs only (no if statements on x):

  • tent(x): 0 outside [−1, 1], rising to 1 at x = 0.
  • bump(x): 0 below −2, rising to 1 by −1, flat at 1 up to 1, back to 0 at 2.
tent(0) == 1, tent(0.5) == 0.5, tent(3) == 0
bump(0) == 1, bump(-1.5) == 0.5, bump(2.5) == 0

tests.name: tent values

hints: Each hinge relu(x - k) adds a corner at k. Its weight changes the slope from that point on.
tent: slope +1 from -1, then -1 from 0 (a change of -2), then 0 from 1 (a change of +1): relu(x+1) - 2*relu(x) + relu(x-1)
